title: Semele
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Opinion is still divided over a goddess's severity when Juno, who will not say whether she blames or approves, hears that Semele of Agenor's house is pregnant by Jupiter — and the hatred she had gathered over a Tyrian rival now spreads to that whole family. Disguised as Semele's old nurse Beroe, she coaches the girl into demanding proof of her lover — let him come to her exactly as he comes to his wife — and since Jupiter has sworn by the Styx he cannot refuse; even the lighter bolt he chooses, the kind the gods call second-rank weapons, is enough to burn her. Watch how the trap is built out of nothing but things a fond nurse might say, and how exact the Latin is about what follows: the unfinished child snatched from the mother's womb and stitched into his father's thigh to serve out her term.

sentences.t:
Rumor in ambiguo est: aliis violentior aequo
visa dea est,
sentences.l: Rumour is in the doubtful: to some the goddess seemed more violent than was fair,
sentences.i: Talk was divided: to some the goddess had been more violent than was fair;
sentences.n: In ambiguo est is literally "is in the doubtful" — the neuter adjective used as a noun, a common Latin way of naming a state. Aequo is an ablative of comparison, "than [what is] fair": Latin can compare with a bare ablative where English needs "than".

sentences.t:
alii laudant dignamque severa
virginitate vocant; pars invenit utraque causas.
sentences.l: others praise her and call her worthy of stern virginity; each of the two parties finds reasons.
sentences.i: others praised her and called her worthy of her stern maidenhood; each side found its grounds.
sentences.n: Dignam takes an ablative of the thing one is worthy of (severa virginitate), and the Latin supplies no possessive with it. Pars utraque, "each of the two parties," is split apart by its own verb — Ovid habitually opens a phrase, drops the verb inside it, and closes it afterwards.

sentences.t:
Sola Iovis coniunx non tam culpetne probetne
eloquitur, quam clade domus ab Agenore ductae
gaudet et a Tyria conlectum paelice transfert
in generis socios odium.
sentences.l: Jove's wife alone does not so much declare whether she blames it or approves it, as she takes joy in the ruin of the house led down from Agenor, and shifts onto the kinsmen of that stock the hatred gathered from that Tyrian mistress.
sentences.i: Jove's wife alone says nothing of blame or approval — she is too busy rejoicing at the ruin of the house descended from Agenor, and turning against its whole kindred the hatred she had stored up over that Tyrian mistress.
sentences.n: Non tam ... quam is "not so much ... as"; culpetne probetne is a double indirect question, "whether she blames or approves." Paelex is a wife's word for the other woman — a rival who has her husband, not a prostitute — and it is Juno's word, not the poem's neutral one: it makes a rival out of Europa, a girl who was carried off from Tyre. The house "led down from Agenor" is Cadmus's, and Semele is of it.

sentences.t:
Subit ecce priori
causa recens, gravidamque dolet de semine magni
esse Iovis Semelen.
sentences.l: Look — a fresh cause comes up beneath the earlier one, and she grieves that Semele is heavy with the seed of great Jove.
sentences.i: And look: a fresh grievance slips in behind the old one — it galls her that Semele is pregnant with great Jove's seed.
sentences.n: Subit priori takes a dative: the compound verb sub- means the new grievance comes up under, i.e. straight after, the old. Dolet is followed by an accusative and infinitive (gravidam ... esse Semelen), "grieves that Semele is pregnant." Semelen is a Greek accusative in -en; Ovid keeps Greek names in Greek case-forms throughout.

sentences.t:
Dum linguam ad iurgia solvit,
“profeci quid enim totiens per iurgia?” dixit:
sentences.l: While she is loosening her tongue for railing, she said: "What indeed have I gained, so many times, by railing?"
sentences.i: As she was loosing her tongue to rail, she said: "And what have all my railings ever gained me?"
sentences.n: Dum with a present indicative describes an action going on in past time — English wants "while she was." Notice the tense shift within one sentence, present solvit beside perfect dixit: Ovid alternates historic present and perfect constantly, speeding the narrative and then setting it down.

sentences.t:
“ipsa petenda mihi est, ipsam, si maxima Iuno
rite vocor, perdam, si me gemmantia dextra
sceptra tenere decet, si sum regina Iovisque
et soror et coniunx, certe soror.
sentences.l: She herself must be gone after by me; her I will destroy — if I am rightly called Juno the greatest, if it befits me to hold the jewelled sceptre in my right hand, if I am queen and Jove's sister and wife both — his sister, at any rate.
sentences.i: It is she I must go after; it is she I will destroy — if I am rightly called Juno most high, if it is proper that my right hand holds the jewelled sceptre, if I am queen, and Jove's sister and wife alike — his sister, at the least.
sentences.n: Petenda mihi est is a gerundive of obligation with a dative of the agent: "must be attacked by me" — an obligation Juno lays on herself, not a prediction. The three si-clauses are courtroom oratory, staked one on another; and the last clause is the bitterest thing Juno says — she and Jupiter are brother and sister as well as husband and wife, and the sisterhood is the half of it he cannot undo.

sentences.t:
At, puto, furto est
contenta, et thalami brevis est iniuria nostri:
sentences.l: But — I suppose — she is content with a theft, and the injury to our marriage-chamber is a short one:
sentences.i: But no doubt she is content with a furtive affair, and the outrage to my marriage bed is a brief one:
sentences.n: Puto dropped in parenthetically is sarcasm, like English "no doubt." Furtum, a theft, is the standard Latin word for a secret love affair — the wrong is framed as property taken. Nostri is the royal plural: Juno means her own bed.

sentences.t:
concipit, id deerat! manifestaque crimina pleno
fert utero,
sentences.l: she conceives — that was the thing missing! — and carries the charges, plain to see, in a full womb,
sentences.i: she conceives — that was the one thing wanting! — and carries the charges against her in plain sight in a swollen belly,
sentences.n: Id deerat is flat sarcasm: "that's all we needed." Crimina is plural, and here it is not the offence but the visible evidence of it — a whole docket of charges, walking about in public. Manifesta is a legal word too, of a crime caught in the act.

sentences.t:
et mater, quod vix mihi contigit uno
de Iove vult fieri: tanta est fiducia formae.
sentences.l: and she wants to be made a mother — a thing that scarcely fell to me, and from Jove alone: so great is her confidence in her beauty.
sentences.i: and she means to be made a mother — a thing that scarcely happened even to me, and I had Jove and no one else: such faith she has in her looks.
sentences.n: Uno de Iove is the sting: Juno has had no partner but her husband, and even so barely bore him a child — though the phrase can equally be taken with vult fieri, "wants to be made a mother by Jove and no one else," and the line, unpunctuated here, will not decide between them. Quod picks up the whole idea of motherhood-by-Jupiter rather than any single word. Fiducia formae is a genitive of the thing trusted in.

sentences.t:
Fallat eam faxo; nec sum Saturnia, si non
ab Iove mersa suo Stygias penetrabit in undas.”
sentences.l: I will see to it that it deceives her; and I am no daughter of Saturn if she does not, sunk by her own Jove, go down into the Stygian waters.
sentences.i: I shall see to it that her beauty betrays her; and Saturn was not my father if she is not sent down, by her own Jove, into the waters of Styx.
sentences.n: Faxo is an old future of facio, "I'll see to it," and takes a bare subjunctive with no ut — a deliberately archaic, oath-like form. The subject of fallat is the fiducia formae of the line before: the thing that will fail her is her confidence in her looks. Mersa means "sunk, drowned," and it is worth remembering when the death arrives, because Semele will die by fire.

sentences.t:
Surgit ab his solio fulvaque recondita nube
limen adit Semeles.
sentences.l: She rises, at these words, from her throne, and, hidden in a tawny cloud, approaches Semele's threshold.
sentences.i: With that she rose from her throne, and, hidden in a tawny cloud, came to Semele's door.
sentences.n: Ab his is "after these words," the neuter plural standing for the speech just given. Semeles is a Greek genitive singular in -es, which Ovid prefers to the Latin Semelae.

sentences.t:
Nec nubes ante removit,
quam simulavit anum posuitque ad tempora canos
sulcavitque cutem rugis et curva trementi
membra tulit passu;
sentences.l: Nor did she take the cloud away before she had counterfeited an old woman, and set grey hair at her temples, and furrowed her skin with wrinkles, and carried bent limbs on a trembling step;
sentences.i: She did not put the cloud aside until she had counterfeited an old woman: grey set at the temples, skin ploughed into wrinkles, bent limbs carried on a shaking step;
sentences.n: Ante ... quam is antequam pulled apart, "before": ante sits near the close of one line and quam opens the next, so the two halves of a single conjunction straddle the verse end. The chain of -que endings piles the disguise on piece by piece; and sulcavit is a farmer's verb, to cut furrows in a field, here used of a face.

sentences.t:
vocem quoque fecit anilem,
ipsaque erat Beroe, Semeles Epidauria nutrix.
sentences.l: she made her voice an old woman's too, and she herself was Beroe, Semele's Epidaurian nurse.
sentences.i: she gave herself an old woman's voice as well — and there she was, Beroe, Semele's nurse from Epidaurus.
sentences.n: Quoque here is the plain adverb "also"; elsewhere in Ovid the same letters are quō-que, "and by which," so it is worth checking each time. Ipsa erat, not "resembled": the disguise is not a likeness but a substitution. Epidaurus lies in the Argolid, the country of Juno's own great cult.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi captato sermone diuque loquendo
ad nomen venere Iovis, suspirat et “opto,
Iuppiter ut sit” ait:
sentences.l: So when, conversation having been angled for and by long talking, they had come to the name of Jove, she sighs and says, "I hope that it is Jupiter":
sentences.i: So when she had drawn the girl into talk, and after long conversation they came round to Jove's name, she sighed and said, "I do hope it is Jupiter";
sentences.n: Captato sermone is an ablative absolute, a self-contained "with X done" phrase where English wants a clause; capto is the frequentative of capio and means to fish for something. Venere is venerunt, the short poetic third-person plural perfect — you will meet it constantly in Ovid (dixere, potuere, dedere).

sentences.t:
“metuo tamen omnia: multi
nomine divorum thalamos iniere pudicos.
sentences.l: but I fear everything: many men have entered chaste bedchambers under the name of gods.
sentences.i: but I fear everything: many a man has got into a chaste bedchamber under a god's name.
sentences.n: Iniere is inierunt, the same short perfect again. Nomine is ablative of means, "under cover of the name." The fear being planted is precisely the fear that will kill Semele — and it is planted by a goddess who is at that moment wearing someone else's face.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen esse Iovem satis est: det pignus amoris,
si modo verus is est,
sentences.l: And yet it is not enough for him to be Jove: let him give a pledge of his love, if only he is the true one,
sentences.i: And even being Jove is not enough: let him give some security for his love — if he really is the true one —
sentences.n: Det is a jussive subjunctive, "let him give." Pignus is a legal term, the security handed over to guarantee a claim; asking a lover for one is cold language, and it is a wife who is putting it in the girl's mouth.

sentences.t:
quantusque et qualis ab alta
Iunone excipitur, tantus talisque, rogato,
det tibi complexus suaque ante insignia sumat.”
sentences.l: and as great and of such a kind as he is received by lofty Juno, just so great and just such — ask it! — let him give you his embrace, and let him take up his own emblems first.
sentences.i: and ask this: that he come into your arms as great and as fully himself as he is when lofty Juno takes him in — just so great, just such — and that he put on his own emblems first.
sentences.n: Quantus ... tantus and qualis ... talis are correlative pairs, "as great as ... so great," "of what sort ... of that sort"; the pair is what makes the demand exact and therefore fatal. Rogato is a future imperative, "you are to ask" — the formal, legal-sounding imperative. The insignia are the thunder and lightning, and the polite periphrasis about embraces is asking for them in bed.

sentences.t:
Talibus ignaram Iuno Cadmeida dictis
formarat.
sentences.l: With such words Juno had shaped the unknowing daughter of Cadmus.
sentences.i: With words like these Juno had moulded the girl of Cadmus's line, who knew nothing of it.
sentences.n: Formarat is formaverat with the -ve- squeezed out, a syncopated pluperfect that is normal in verse. Cadmeida is a Greek patronymic accusative, "the daughter of Cadmus" — Semele. Note where ignaram sits: enclosed inside talibus ... dictis, the very words that are doing the shaping.

sentences.t:
Rogat illa Iovem sine nomine munus.
Cui deus “elige” ait: “nullam patiere repulsam.
sentences.l: She asks Jove a gift without a name. And to her the god says, "Choose: you will suffer no refusal.
sentences.i: She asked Jove for a gift and did not name it. "Choose," the god said to her; "you shall meet no refusal.
sentences.n: Rogo takes two accusatives, the person asked and the thing asked for: rogat Iovem munus. Cui opens the sentence as a connecting relative — Latin loves to begin a new sentence with a relative pronoun where English says "and to her." Patiere is patieris, the alternative second-singular passive ending, common in poetry.

sentences.t:
Quoque magis credas, Stygii quoque conscia sunto
numina torrentis: timor et deus ille deorum est“.
sentences.l: And that you may believe it the more, let the powers of the Stygian torrent also be witness to it: that one is both the terror and the god of the gods."
sentences.i: And so that you may believe it the more, let the powers of the Stygian flood stand witness too: that stream is the gods' own terror, and their god."
sentences.n: Both quoque-shapes stand in this one sentence: the first is quō-que, quo + magis with a subjunctive of purpose ("and so that you may the more"), the second is the ordinary adverb "also." Sunto is the archaic third-person future imperative, the form used in laws and oaths. The oath sworn on the Styx is the one no god may break, which is why nothing after this can be called back. One further oddity is the archive's and not ours: the edition closes this speech with a reversed quotation mark, and Lectorium prints its witness as it stands.

sentences.t:
Laeta malo nimiumque potens perituraque amantis
obsequio Semele “qualem Saturnia” dixit
“te solet amplecti, Veneris cum foedus initis,
da mihi te talem.”
sentences.l: Glad at her own harm, and too powerful, and about to perish by her lover's compliance, Semele said: "Such as Saturnia is used to embrace you, when the two of you enter the compact of Venus — give yourself such to me."
sentences.i: Glad at what would destroy her, too powerful for her own good, doomed by her lover's obedience, Semele said: "Come to me as Saturnia is used to holding you, when the two of you enter the treaty of Venus — come to me just so."
sentences.n: Three phrases are stacked in front of the subject, and every one of them is the narrator seeing the end before she does: laeta malo, "glad at her own ruin," and peritura, "about to die." Obsequio is an ablative of means — the instrument of her death is his willingness to do as she asks. Foedus Veneris, "the compact of Venus," is treaty language used of going to bed, and initis is second-person plural: the treaty has two parties to it.

sentences.t:
Voluit deus ora loquentis
opprimere: exierat iam vox properata sub auras.
sentences.l: The god wanted to press shut the mouth of her as she spoke: the hurried voice had already gone out into the air.
sentences.i: The god would have shut her mouth as she spoke: the words had already rushed out into the open air.
sentences.n: Voluit is "wanted, wished" — not "tried": the pluperfect exierat does the timing all by itself, and by the time he wanted it the thing was already gone. Loquentis is a participle used as a noun in the genitive, "of her speaking." Properata, "hurried," belongs to Semele but is attached to her voice — a transferred epithet.

sentences.t:
Ingemuit; neque enim non haec optasse, neque ille
non iurasse potest.
sentences.l: He groaned; for neither can she not have wished [it], nor he not have sworn [it].
sentences.i: He groaned: she cannot un-wish it, and he cannot un-swear it.
sentences.n: The double negatives are exact: non potest non optasse is "cannot not-have-wished," that is, the wish is now a fact beyond anyone's reach, and the idiomatic layer says the same thing with un-wish and un-swear. Optasse and iurasse are syncopated perfect infinitives for optavisse, iuravisse — both acts are finished ones. Haec and ille — she and he — stand one in each neque-clause and crossed about their negatives (non haec ... ille non), so the balance of the sentence is the balance of their two guilts. The object of both infinitives is unexpressed in the Latin, which is why the literal brackets it.

sentences.t:
Ergo maestissimus altum
aethera conscendit vultuque sequentia traxit
nubila, quis nimbos inmixtaque fulgura ventis
addidit et tonitrus et inevitabile fulmen.
sentences.l: So, in the deepest grief, he climbed the high upper air and with his face drew the clouds that followed, and to them he added rainstorms and lightnings mixed with winds and thunder and the bolt there is no escaping.
sentences.i: So, in the depth of his grief, he climbed into the high air and drew the clouds after him with a look, and added to them storm-rain, lightning tangled in wind, thunder, and the bolt from which there is no escape.
sentences.n: Conscendit can be present or perfect; beside the plain perfect traxit it reads as perfect here, and both layers render it so. Aethera is a Greek accusative in -a; Ovid keeps the Greek endings of Greek words. Quis is an old form of quibus, and it opens its clause as a connecting relative, "and to these." The clouds follow his expression: for a sky-god, a mood and the weather are the same event.

sentences.l: Yet as far as he is able, he tries to take strength away from himself; and he does not now arm himself with the fire with which he had struck down hundred-handed Typhoeus: there is too much savagery in that one.
sentences.i: Still, so far as he can, he tries to subtract his own power; and he does not arm himself now with the fire that brought down hundred-handed Typhoeus: there is too much wildness in it.
sentences.n: Sibi is a dative of separation with demere, "take away from himself" — Latin uses a dative where English says "from." The relative clause comes before the word it modifies (quo ... igne ... eo), which is normal in verse and worth reading twice. Typhoea is a Greek accusative; centimanum, "hundred-handed," is the epithet Ovid gives the monster here.

sentences.l: There is another, lighter bolt, into which the right hand of the Cyclopes put less of savagery and flame, less of anger; the gods above call them the second weapons.
sentences.i: There is a second bolt, a lighter one, into which the Cyclopes' hand put less cruelty and fire, less rage; the gods call these the weapons of the second rank.
sentences.n: Levius is a comparative — another, lighter bolt, not the lightest he owns — and tela secunda is a plural, a whole class of weapon rather than a single one. Saevitiae, flammae and irae are partitive genitives after minus, "less of savagery," and the repetition of minus does the measuring. The Cyclopes are Jupiter's smiths, so the thunderbolt is a manufactured object — and this passage quietly gives heaven an armoury with a lighter shelf on it.

sentences.t:
Capit illa, domumque
intrat Agenoream. Corpus mortale tumultus
non tulit aetherios donisque iugalibus arsit.
sentences.l: He takes those, and enters the house of Agenor. A mortal body did not bear the upheavals of heaven, and she burned with the gifts of her bridal.
sentences.i: He took those, and entered the house of Agenor. A mortal body could not bear the tumult of the sky, and she burned with her wedding gifts.
sentences.n: Illa is neuter plural, picking up the tela secunda of the line before — he takes the lighter weapons, and they are still enough. Domus Agenorea is Cadmus's house named from its Tyrian founder. Donis iugalibus is the cruel phrase: the thunder and lightning she asked for as proof of love are entered here as the presents of a wedding.

sentences.t:
Imperfectus adhuc infans genetricis ab alvo
eripitur, patrioque tener (si credere dignum est)
insuitur femori maternaque tempora complet.
sentences.l: The child, still unfinished, is snatched from his mother's belly, and, tender as he is (if the thing deserves belief), he is stitched into his father's thigh and fills out his mother's full term.
sentences.i: The infant, not yet finished, is torn from his mother's womb and — if the thing deserves belief — is sewn, tender as he is, into his father's thigh, where he serves out the months his mother would have carried.
sentences.n: Imperfectus is meant literally, "not yet completed": the pregnancy, not the child's character. Insuitur is in + suo, "is stitched into," a needle-and-thread word for a needle-and-thread operation, and materna tempora are the months of gestation still owing, now served in the thigh. The parenthesis is Ovid flagging the tallest claim in the tale himself, rather than asking us to swallow it.

sentences.t:
Furtim illum primis Ino matertera cuuis
educat:
sentences.l: In secret his mother's sister Ino rears him in his first [cradle?]:
sentences.i: In secret Ino, his mother's sister, brought him up in his first [cradle?]:
sentences.n: The digitization of the 1892 edition is damaged at the last word of the first line here: it prints cuuis, which is not a Latin word at all. Other editions read cunis, the ablative plural of cunae, "cradle" — primis cunis, "in his first cradle" — and that is what the sense of the line requires. Both translation layers therefore bracket the word as [cradle?]: the English there is supplied from the sense of the line, not read off the form in front of you. Lectorium prints its witness as it stands and tells you where it fails, rather than mending the text silently. Matertera is specifically a mother's sister: Ino and Semele are both daughters of Cadmus.

sentences.t:
inde datum nymphae Nyseides antris
occuluere suis lactisque alimenta dedere.
sentences.l: then, [him] handed over, the nymphs of Nysa hid him in caves of their own and gave him the nourishment of milk.
sentences.i: then he was handed on, and the nymphs of Nysa hid him away in caves of their own and fed him on milk.
sentences.n: Datum is a perfect participle in the accusative, agreeing with the illum of the line before — the child, not the nymphs — and it does the work of a whole English clause, "after he had been given over." Occuluere and dedere are venerunt-style short perfects again (occuluerunt, dederunt) — four of them now in this part. Nyseides is a Greek feminine plural, "the Nysean ones": Nysa is where the child Bacchus is nursed.
